title: How to thread a needle
subtitle: Getting thread through the eye cleanly, first time.
excerpt: Threading a needle takes five seconds once you know the knack. The thread needs to be cut cleanly at an angle, the end slightly moistened, and the needle held still rather than chased across the thread.
sourceNotes:

glossaryTerms.definition: The hole at the blunt end of a needle through which the thread passes. On tapestry needles the eye is elongated to accommodate multiple strands of stranded cotton; on sharps the eye is smaller and more oval.
Embroidery thread made of six individual strands loosely twisted together. The six strands are separated before threading so the stitcher can use one, two, or more strands as the pattern requires.

content.text: Threading a needle is a matter of holding the needle still and bringing the thread to it. Most people do it the wrong way round, chasing the needle with the thread, which is why it takes a dozen attempts. Cut the thread end at a sharp angle, moisten it slightly, and push it through the
needle eye
while pinching the needle steady between thumb and finger.
What you need

items.name: Stranded cotton, separated to the strand count needed

content.text: Threading by hand
Separate the correct number of strands from the
stranded cotton
skein before you cut. Then:
Cut the thread to your working length. About 40 to 50 cm is the standard; longer threads tangle and weaken with repeated pulling through cloth.
Use embroidery scissors to cut the end at a 45-degree angle. A flat cut frays immediately; the angled cut gives you a firm tip.
Moisten the cut end lightly, either on your lip or with a barely damp fingertip. This pulls the fibres together into a narrow tip.
Hold the needle between thumb and forefinger of your dominant hand with the eye facing upward. Do not move the needle.
Bring the thread end to the eye from the front and push it through in one steady movement. Pull about 8 to 10 cm through, leaving a short tail.
Using a needle threader
Push the wire loop of the threader through the needle eye from the front.
Pass the thread through the wire loop.
Draw the threader back through the eye, pulling the thread with it.
Pull the thread end through until about 8 to 10 cm remains as a tail.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: What goes wrong
attrs.intro: Three problems that make threading take longer than it should.

items.cause: The needle is moving as the thread approaches it.
items.fix: Pin the needle to a cushion or hold it firmly against your thumbnail with the eye up. Bring the thread to the still needle rather than chasing a moving target.

items.symptom: Thread end splays and won't go through
items.cause: The cut was straight across, or the thread is dry.
items.fix: Re-cut at 45 degrees and moisten the end. Pressing the cut end flat between your thumbnail and finger before attempting to thread also helps.

items.symptom: Thread slips out of the eye after threading
items.cause: Too short a tail was left through the eye.
items.fix: Leave at least 8 cm of tail. For slippery threads such as metallic, leave 12 to 15 cm.

content.text: What this underpins
Threading is the first step in every embroidery technique. A solid
threading technique
also makes needle threaders useful on tiny needle eyes where the wire loop does the work.
